questions.question: Why is reading a local variable inside a function typically faster than reading a global?
options: Locals are fixed array slots (LOAD_FAST), while globals and built-ins need dictionary lookups (LOAD_GLOBAL)
Locals are compiled to machine code but globals are not
Globals are protected by a separate lock
questions.explanation: The compiler assigns each local a slot in the frame, so access is an index; globals require dict lookups in the module and builtins namespaces.

questions.question: After a function multiplies floats many times, `dis.dis(fn, adaptive=True)` shows BINARY_OP_MULTIPLY_FLOAT instead of BINARY_OP. What explains this?
options: The JIT compiler is always enabled
The .pyc file was rewritten on disk
The specializing adaptive interpreter (PEP 659) rewrote the instruction for the types it observed
dis shows a different function each time
questions.explanation: Since Python 3.11, hot instructions are specialized in place for the types they see, skipping generic dispatch.

questions.question: What is the status of the free-threaded (no-GIL) build in Python 3.14?
options: Officially supported but optional; the default build still has the GIL
It is the default interpreter on all platforms
questions.explanation: PEP 779 made the free-threaded build officially supported in 3.14, but it remains a separate, optional build.

questions.question: Which is a genuine trade-off of running on the free-threaded build?
options: Bytecode can no longer be inspected with dis
All C extensions run unchanged with no GIL
Single-threaded code runs somewhat slower, and C extensions without free-threading support cause the GIL to be re-enabled
questions.explanation: The no-GIL build carries some single-threaded overhead, and importing an extension that has not declared support turns the GIL back on.
